name: Wheatgrass diet

lead: The wheatgrass diet centres on juice pressed from young shoots of wheat, usually drunk fresh as a shot or as the core of a raw-food or detox plan. Practitioners link it to clearer-looking skin, more energy and a generally healthier appearance through its chlorophyll, vitamins and antioxidants.

The idea dates to the 1930s and was popularised by Ann Wigmore's Hippocrates Health Institute. Research is limited to small trials and rodent studies on outcomes such as antioxidant status; no trial has measured appearance.

paras: People juice fresh wheatgrass or buy it as a shot, powder or tablet, often alongside other raw foods. Wigmore-style programs make it a daily staple. Hobbyists on strength-training forums describe adding a shot to a day, or using greens powders, for alertness and general wellbeing.

The American Cancer Society states that available scientific evidence does not support wheatgrass preventing or curing disease. Safety guidance in the literature stresses hygienic cultivation, a pesticide-free growing medium and testing for microbes and heavy metals, and juice is meant to be drunk soon after pressing.

chain: Fresh wheatgrass juice supplies chlorophyll, vitamins and antioxidant compounds
Proponents say this supports detoxification and overall health
angle.text: People drink wheatgrass juice in the hope that its antioxidants and nutrients will show in their skin, energy and overall look. This is the proponents' account; no study has measured appearance outcomes.

lead: The wheatgrass diet is a regimen in which juice from young wheat shoots (Triticum aestivum) is a daily staple, either alone or as part of a raw-food program. Followers see it as a way to detoxify and nourish the body, with benefits they associate with clearer skin, energy and a healthier look.[1]

Wheatgrass drinking in the West is credited to Charles Schnabel in the 1930s, whose powdered grass was sold in North American drugstores by 1940. Ann Wigmore, founder of the Hippocrates Health Institute, later promoted it as part of a raw-food diet and said it cleansed toxins and helped treat serious illness.[1]

Research consists of small, often short human trials in conditions such as thalassemia, inflammatory bowel disease and chemotherapy side effects, plus animal and laboratory studies, and reviews call for larger trials.[1][2] The American Cancer Society states that evidence does not support wheatgrass curing or preventing disease.[1]
infobox: Charles Schnabel (1930s); Ann Wigmore, Hippocrates Health Institute
Chlorophyll, amino acids, minerals, vitamins, antioxidant enzymes; no vitamin B12

paras: Wheatgrass is the young, germinated shoot of the wheat plant. It contains chlorophyll, amino acids, minerals, vitamins and antioxidant enzymes, and does not contain vitamin B12.[1] In rodent work, a wheatgrass extract showed its highest antioxidant potential at nine days after germination, and nine flavonoids were identified in it.[2]
Practitioners prefer cold-pressed juice drunk within minutes of pressing, because heat and blending are said to degrade nutrients.[1]

Charles Schnabel is credited with starting Western consumption of wheatgrass in the 1930s, and his powder was sold in drugstores in the US and Canada by 1940.[1] Ann Wigmore later made it central to the raw-food program at the Hippocrates Health Institute, saying it cleansed the body of toxins.[1]

On T Nation forums, a poster who juices wheatgrass at home describes feeling more awake and alert during the day without an energy spike afterward, while allowing that it coincided with a change in eating habits.[3] Other members list wheatgrass among their general supplements, and a 2025 forum item discusses greens powders in general.[4][5]
The literature emphasises hygienic cultivation, pesticide-free growing medium, and microbial and heavy-metal testing of the grass and juice.[1]

Small trials summarised in reviews report possible benefits such as reduced transfusion needs in thalassemia, fewer chemotherapy side effects, and improvements in some inflammatory bowel disease measures, with modest antioxidant changes; reviewers urge cautious interpretation and larger trials.[1] A 2021 study in diabetic rats fed a wheatgrass diet for 60 days reported improvements in oxidative-stress markers; this is animal research.[2] No human study has measured skin or appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: Wheatgrass appears in forum conversation as a green-juice habit for energy and general health.[3]
